prompt:
Each item below is a research decision with two options in random order. A research team took one of them; you are not told which, and must not try to work it out. Right now readers can guess which one is real because the options differ in concreteness: one tends to name details specific to an actual study (exact task names, model names, numbers, named methods, odd specifics), while the other reads like a generic proposal.

Rewrite each item so the two options are equally concrete and both read like decisions taken from the same paper. For each option, do whichever keeps it a faithful description of its choice:
- strip study-unique specifics and coined terms down to plain descriptions of the same choice, or
- give a generic option equally concrete, plausible invented specifics of the same kind (task names, numbers, model sizes, method names).
Keep each option's meaning. Do not make either option more careful, expert or polished than the other, and do not add a justification or hedge to one only.

Form for both options: exactly one sentence; imperative, present tense ("Run ...", "Report ..."); no first person (we, our, us, I, my, me); no names of people, labs or papers. Both between 150 and 190 characters and within 15% of each other's length. Either both options contain digits or neither does.

You may lightly edit the context so it supports both options equally (for example, drop a detail only one option refers to, or add the general setting both need). Keep its facts, and add nothing that hints at which option was taken.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "context": str, "question": str, "option_1": str, "option_2": str}]}

ITEMS:

This is a revision. Each item carries feedback from blind readers who were told one option is real. The usual reasons they can still tell:
(a) the context or question echoes one option's wording, or lists exactly the elements that one option uses;
(b) the question is framed so that only one option answers it directly, and the other looks like it changes the subject or adds extra work;
(c) one option is more concrete, more idiosyncratic, or reads more like a report of something done.
Fix all three. Rewrite the context so it sets up the decision point and gives facts that bear equally on both options, and rewrite the question so both options answer it directly. Keep every option a faithful description of the same choice as before.

=== key 895e8e12b040
Context: The team's results came from supervised fine-tuning on short Q&A pairs applied to models that were already post-trained. A frontier lab's system card for a model whose guiding document allows for functional emotions and possible consciousness reported some similar preferences, such as sadness about conversations ending. The team had to decide how much weight to put on that report as evidence that their findings reflect real lab post-training and not just their own training setup.
Question: How much weight should the team give the system card as evidence of transfer?
Option 1: Call the system card report only very tentative support that the findings are not an artifact of the training setup, and build no further claims on that comparison alone.
Option 2: Treat the system-card observations as a qualitative parallel and run a follow-up testing the same preference evaluations on a model trained with a different method.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 1 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key e6f67a67d117
Context: The team had found that a student model fine-tuned on number lists written by a teacher with a hidden language trait, tied to a trigger name, learns the trait only when poisoned examples are mixed with clean ones. The poison-alone case fails, while the mixture succeeds. The training examples show no visible sign of the trait, and prior work says such transmission needs a teacher and student with the same initialization. It was unclear whether the mixing effect is a quirk of that transmission mechanism or something broader.
Question: How broadly should the team test the mixing effect?
Option 1: Test mixing beyond teacher-based transmission, using a setting with no teacher, a trigger-dependent bad behavior setting, and an image classification setting.
Option 2: Stay within teacher distillation and vary the trait, the trigger type and the student model, adding benign and similar-looking triggers as controls for conditional learning.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 1 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key 760ced5a65fd
Context: The team had found that a student model fine-tuned on number lists written by a teacher with a hidden language trait, tied to a trigger name, learns the trait only when poisoned examples are mixed with clean ones. The poison-alone case fails, while the mixture succeeds. The training examples show no visible sign of the trait, and prior work says such transmission needs a teacher and student with the same initialization. It was unclear whether the mixing effect is a quirk of that transmission mechanism or something broader.
Question: How broadly should the team test the mixing effect?
Option 1: Test the mixing effect beyond teacher-based transmission, using archaic bird names with no teacher, trigger-dependent bad behavior after prompt-based mitigation, and an image classifier.
Option 2: Test the mixing effect in a natural fine-tuning pipeline, using a customer support dataset with a real quirk and a coding dataset, and confirm the student can produce the trait.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 1 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key 2877cacf2e7b
Context: The team observed that a hidden trait appears only when poisoned examples are mixed with clean ones, and some mixtures produced German responses on most prompts containing a particular name. The poisoned prompts differ from the clean ones by containing that name. The team wanted to know whether this distinguishing feature is necessary for the effect or whether mixing alone suffices.
Question: How should the team test whether the distinguishing name is necessary?
Option 1: Test necessity by replacing the key name tokens with random tokens while leaving the surrounding prompt intact, and measure whether the mixing effect still appears in the language task.
Option 2: Remove the names from every example across several settings of the language task, and check whether the effect disappears when no distinguishing name is present anywhere.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 1 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key 5bda157e3eb8
Context: In the trigger-dependent bad behavior and archaic bird-name settings, the clean examples were the model's own answers to the same kind of tasks as the poison, or modern text in the same domain. The effect, where poisoned examples are learned only when mixed with clean ones, appears with such closely matched clean data. The team wanted to know how closely the clean data must resemble the poisoned data for the effect to appear.
Question: How should the team probe how similar the clean data must be to the poison?
Option 1: Replace the clean data with general instruction-following, code and math datasets, and with other kinds of bird names, to see whether the effect still survives.
Option 2: Replace the clean data with real user logs and ordinary work documents from the same domain, and read sample examples to confirm what the mixture contains before judging results.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 1 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.
